div.head: Ps Cn for 19
div.ab: Si quis mediocrium aliquem ictu cum ira percusserit, emendetur, prout interfectio fere regalis mihi emendari solet.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 623 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)
div.ab: If anyone strikes one of the middling men with a blow in anger, let compensation be paid as compensation is usually paid to me for the killing of a royal beast.

note.seg: c̄ira wohl nicht wie o. 104 aus īcꝛia verderbt
c̄ira: probably not, as above at 10 note 4, a corruption of īcꝛia (in curia)

d. h. absichtlich im Germanischen Recht; Brunner II 544. 561; vgl. Freibrief Bolton's a. 1253 (ed. Bateson Engl. hist. rev. 1902, 291): si quis burgensem per iram percusserit absque sanguinis effusione. Volkshass führte wohl oft zu Gewaltthat gegen Forstbeamte

i.e. 'intentionally' in Germanic law; Brunner II 544. 561; compare Bolton's charter of liberties of 1253 (ed. Bateson Engl. hist. rev. 1902, 291): si quis burgensem per iram percusserit absque sanguinis effusione. Popular hatred probably often led to violence against forest officials

das vornehmste Forstthier, den Hirsch, bewerthen die Normannenkönige dem Menschen gleich, wie Verf. hier und unten 25. 34, und strafen dessen Erlegung mit Verstümmelung, dem Ersatz der Todesstrafe, worüber die damalige Literatur laut klagt: Ann. Anglosax. 1086; Ioh. Saresber. Polycrat. I 4; Galfr. Monm. VII 3; Vita Haroldi 12 (ed. Birch 64); Will. Neuburg. I 3. Wer den jagenden König malt, setzt einen Hirsch davor; s. das Bild bei Hall Courtlife under Plantagenets

The Norman kings valued the noblest beast of the forest, the stag, equal to a man, as the author does here and below 25. 34, and punished its killing with mutilation, the substitute for the death penalty, of which the literature of the time loudly complains: Ann. Anglosax. 1086; Ioh. Saresber. Polycrat. I 4; Galfr. Monm. VII 3; Vita Haroldi 12 (ed. Birch 64); Will. Neuburg. I 3. Whoever paints the king hunting puts a stag before him; see the picture in Hall Courtlife under Plantagenets
